breakfast.name: Hoppers (Appa)
instructions: Dissolve yeast and sugar in warm water and let it froth for 10 minutes.
Mix rice flour with coconut milk and the yeast mixture to form a smooth batter.
Add salt and let the batter ferment for at least 8 hours or overnight.
Heat a small hopper pan and grease lightly with coconut oil.
Pour a ladleful of batter and swirl the pan to coat the sides thinly.
Crack an egg into the center, cover and cook on low heat until the edges are crispy and the egg is set.
Serve hot with coconut sambol or lunu miris.
breakfast.description: Bowl-shaped rice flour crepes with crispy lacy edges and a soft center, often served with an egg nestled inside. A beloved Sri Lankan breakfast staple.

breakfast.name: Kiribath (Milk Rice)
instructions: Wash rice thoroughly and cook with water in a heavy-bottomed pot until almost done.
Pour in the thick coconut milk and salt, stir gently.
Cook on low heat, stirring occasionally, until the milk is fully absorbed and the rice is creamy.
Flatten the rice into a square or rectangular shape on a flat plate.
Allow to cool slightly, then cut into diamond shapes.
Serve with lunu miris (chili onion relish) or jaggery.
breakfast.description: Creamy coconut milk rice traditionally prepared for Sinhala New Year and auspicious occasions. Cut into diamond shapes and served with spicy sambol.

breakfast.name: String Hoppers (Idiyappam) with Coconut Milk
instructions: String hoppers are the Sri Lankan breakfast -- delicate rice noodle nests
Made by pressing rice flour dough through a special mold with small holes
The dough is pressed out in a circular pattern onto a hopper mat
Steamed for a few minutes
The result: a delicate, lacy noodle nest
Served with fresh coconut milk poured over -- the morning version
Or with coconut sambal, dhal, or curry
String hoppers (idiyappam) are also eaten in Tamil Nadu, India
The Sri Lankan and South Indian food connection across the Palk Strait
breakfast.description: Sri Lankan steamed rice noodle nests -- rice flour dough pressed through a special mold into circular noodle nests, steamed until delicate, served with fresh coconut milk or coconut sambal. Called idiyappam in Tamil. The lacy, delicate texture is the craft. Eaten across the Palk Strait into Tamil Nadu.

breakfast.name: Milk Rice (Kiribath)
instructions: Kiribath (milk rice) is the Sri Lankan celebration and auspicious food
Rice cooked in thick coconut milk until very soft and cohesive
Pressed into a square tray and cut into diamond shapes
Eaten on auspicious occasions: New Year (Sinhala and Tamil New Year), first day of school, weddings
On the Sinhala New Year (April 13-14), kiribath is the first food eaten after the auspicious time
The white color: auspicious and pure
Eaten with lunu miris (spicy onion-chilli paste) -- the contrast of white rice and red paste
breakfast.description: Sri Lankan ceremonial coconut milk rice -- short-grain rice cooked in thick coconut milk until cohesive, pressed and cut into diamonds. The auspicious food for Sinhala and Tamil New Year (April 13-14), first day of school, and weddings. The white color is auspicious; eaten with spicy lunu miris paste for contrast.

lunch.name: Rice and Curry
instructions: Cook rice until fluffy and set aside.
Heat coconut oil in a clay pot or heavy saucepan. Add cinnamon, cardamom, and curry leaves.
Sauté onion until golden, then add garlic, ginger, and green chilies.
Add curry powder and turmeric, stir for 30 seconds.
Add chicken pieces and coat well with the spice mixture.
Pour in coconut milk and tamarind paste. Season with salt.
Simmer on low heat for 35-40 minutes until chicken is tender and the curry has thickened.
Serve the curry over steamed rice with accompaniments like dhal, gotukola sambol, and papadum.
lunch.description: The quintessential Sri Lankan meal featuring fragrant rice surrounded by an array of curries, sambols, and accompaniments, each with distinct flavors.

lunch.name: Kottu Roti
ingredients: 4 godamba roti or flatbreads, torn into pieces
instructions: Heat oil on a flat griddle or large pan over high heat.
Add curry leaves and sauté leeks, carrots, and cabbage until slightly softened.
Add shredded chicken and stir-fry for 2 minutes.
Toss in the torn roti pieces and mix well.
Season with curry powder, chili flakes, soy sauce, salt, and pepper.
Push mixture to one side, pour beaten eggs on the griddle and scramble.
Chop and mix everything together using two metal spatulas, creating the signature rhythmic chopping sound.
Serve hot with a side of curry sauce.
lunch.description: Chopped godamba roti stir-fried with vegetables, egg, and spices on a hot griddle. The rhythmic chopping sound of kottu being made is iconic in Sri Lankan street food culture.

lunch.name: Kottu Roti (Chopped Roti Stir-Fry)
ingredients: Godamba roti (thin, flaky flatbread -- Sri Lankan paratha-style)
instructions: Kottu roti is the Sri Lankan street food sound -- the rhythmic metal-on-metal chopping
The gotcha roti is chopped on a hot griddle with two metal blades
The rhythmic chopping: you hear the kottu restaurant before you see it
Mixed with egg, vegetables, and meat while chopping
The roti strips absorb the curry flavors
A cheap, filling, and deeply satisfying street food
Every Sri Lankan street has a kottu vendor at night
lunch.description: Sri Lankan chopped flatbread stir-fry -- godamba roti chopped on a hot griddle with two metal blades in a rhythmic clatter (you hear the kottu vendor before you see it), mixed with egg, vegetables, and curry powder. The street sound of Sri Lanka. Every Sri Lankan street has a kottu vendor at night.

lunch.name: Pol Sambol (Coconut Sambal)
ingredients: Maldive fish (dried tuna flakes -- optional but traditional)
instructions: Pol sambol is the Sri Lankan coconut sambal -- eaten at every meal
Fresh grated coconut mixed with spicy, acidic ingredients
The Maldive fish: dried, cured tuna from the Maldives -- the umami element
Trade route history: Sri Lanka and the Maldives traded dried fish for centuries
The combination: coconut + onion + chilli + lime + Maldive fish
Eaten with rice, hoppers, string hoppers, bread -- everything
No Sri Lankan meal is complete without pol sambol
lunch.description: Sri Lankan coconut sambal -- fresh grated coconut mixed with red onion, dried chilli, lime juice, and Maldive fish (dried cured tuna from the Maldives: centuries of island trade). The essential Sri Lankan condiment. No Sri Lankan meal is complete without pol sambol.

lunch.name: Fish Ambulthiyal (Sour Fish Curry)
ingredients: Goraka (gamboge -- a dried sour fruit, Garcinia cambogia relative)
instructions: Ambulthiyal is the Sri Lankan sour fish curry -- preserved fish using goraka
Goraka: a dried sour fruit (Garcinia cambogia relative) -- the souring and preserving agent
The fish is coated in a goraka paste and slow-cooked very dry
The very low moisture content means it keeps for days without refrigeration
A traveling food: sailors took it on long voyages
The black pepper and goraka combination gives an intense, sour-spicy coating
The smell of goraka: intensely sour, almost unpleasant raw -- beautiful when cooked
lunch.description: Sri Lankan sour-dried fish curry -- tuna coated in a goraka paste (dried Garcinia relative, intensely sour), black pepper, and turmeric, cooked very dry until almost no moisture remains. Preserved without refrigeration for days. A sailor food: taken on long Indian Ocean voyages. The goraka sourness is the dish identity.

dinner.name: Lamprais
instructions: Cook rice in meat stock with cardamom, cloves, and cinnamon until fluffy.
Prepare the mixed meat curry by browning meat in ghee, adding lamprais curry powder, coconut milk, and simmering until tender.
Make the ash plantain curry with coconut milk and spices.
Prepare the blachan sambol by roasting shrimp paste with onions, chili, and Maldive fish.
Soften banana leaves over a flame until pliable.
Place a portion of rice in each banana leaf, top with meat curry, ash plantain, blachan sambol, and a hard-boiled egg.
Wrap into tight parcels and bake at 180°C for 20 minutes.
Serve the parcels whole, unwrapping at the table.
dinner.description: A Dutch-Burgher heritage dish of rice and curries wrapped in banana leaf and baked. Each parcel contains a complete meal of fragrant rice, rich meat curry, and accompaniments.

dinner.name: Fish Ambul Thiyal (Sour Fish Curry)
instructions: Rub tuna cubes with goraka paste, turmeric, black pepper, and salt. Marinate for 15 minutes.
Place marinated fish in a clay pot. Add curry leaves, garlic, pandan leaf, fenugreek, and cinnamon.
Add just enough water to barely cover the fish.
Cook on medium heat without stirring, gently shaking the pot occasionally.
Reduce heat and simmer until all the liquid evaporates and the fish is coated in a dark, thick glaze.
The fish should be dry-cooked and deeply flavored.
Serve with steamed rice and coconut sambol.
dinner.description: A signature Southern Sri Lankan dry fish curry with an intensely sour and spicy flavor from goraka. This preserved dish can last for days without refrigeration.

dinner.name: Hoppers (Appa) with Egg
ingredients: Rice flour (fermented overnight with coconut milk and yeast)
instructions: Hoppers (appa) are the Sri Lankan bowl-shaped rice crêpes
Made from a fermented rice flour batter
Cooked in a small wok (the hopper pan) -- the round shape forms the bowl
The edge is crispy and lacy; the center is soft and thick
Egg hopper: an egg is cracked into the hopper before it sets
The egg white sets but the yolk stays runny
The combination of crispy edge, soft center, and runny yolk
Eaten with coconut sambal and curry
dinner.description: Sri Lankan bowl-shaped rice crêpe -- fermented rice flour batter swirled in a small round wok, creating a crispy-lacy edge and soft center. Egg hopper: an egg cracked in before the batter sets, the yolk staying runny. Eaten with coconut sambal and curry. The hopper pan shape is the technique.

dinner.name: Dhal (Red Lentil Curry)
instructions: Sri Lankan dhal is made with red lentils and coconut milk
The tempering: mustard seeds crackled in oil with curry leaves and dried chilli
The tempering is poured over the cooked lentils -- the sizzle, the fragrance
Curry leaves: the essential Sri Lankan aromatic herb
Coconut milk stirs in at the end for richness
Eaten with every Sri Lankan rice meal -- the essential side dish
dinner.description: Sri Lankan coconut milk dhal -- red lentils simmered with turmeric and chilli, finished with a tempering (mustard seeds crackled in oil with curry leaves and dried chilli poured sizzling over), and coconut milk stirred in. Curry leaves are the essential Sri Lankan aromatic. Eaten with every Sri Lankan rice meal.

dinner.name: Wambatu Moju (Pickled Eggplant)
instructions: Wambatu moju is the Sri Lankan pickled eggplant -- sweet, sour, and spicy
The eggplant is deep-fried first -- until golden and slightly crispy
Then combined with vinegar, sugar, and spices
The sweet-sour-spicy balance is the Sri Lankan flavor profile
Moju means pickle in Sinhala
A condiment alongside rice and curries
dinner.description: Sri Lankan sweet-sour pickled eggplant -- eggplant fried until golden, combined with vinegar, sugar, and mustard seeds, tossed with fried onion and chilli. Sweet, sour, and spicy: the Sri Lankan flavor balance. Moju means pickle in Sinhala.

snacks.name: Isso Vadei (Prawn Fritters)
instructions: Drain and grind soaked urad dhal into a thick, smooth paste.
Mix in chopped onion, green chilies, curry leaves, cumin, and salt.
Shape small portions of the dhal paste into flat rounds.
Press a prawn into the top of each fritter with the tail sticking out.
Deep fry in hot oil until golden and crispy on both sides.
Drain on paper towels.
Serve hot with chili sauce or lunu miris.
snacks.description: Crispy lentil fritters topped with whole prawns, a beloved Sri Lankan street snack. The contrast of crunchy dhal and succulent prawn makes them irresistible.

snacks.name: Isso Wade (Prawn Lentil Patties)
ingredients: Prawn (one per patty, placed on top)
Onion, garlic, curry leaves, chilli, ginger
instructions: Isso wade are the Sri Lankan prawn-topped lentil fritters
A seasoned lentil paste formed into discs
A prawn is pressed onto the top of each patty
Fried until golden -- the prawn curls and turns orange on top
A crunchy outer shell from the lentil
Sold in Colombo as street food -- especially at the Galle Face Green
snacks.description: Sri Lankan prawn lentil fritters -- seasoned chana dhal paste formed into discs with a prawn pressed on top, fried until golden and crunchy (the prawn curls and turns orange). Sold at Galle Face Green in Colombo. The lentil crust is the container for the prawn.

snacks.name: Coconut Roti (Pol Roti)
instructions: Pol roti is the Sri Lankan coconut flatbread
A simple dough with fresh grated coconut mixed in
Cooked on a flat pan until slightly charred
The coconut creates an irregular texture and slight sweetness
Eaten for breakfast or as a snack with sambal
Thicker and heavier than Indian roti -- the coconut adds bulk
snacks.description: Sri Lankan coconut flatbread -- flour dough with fresh grated coconut, onion, and green chilli mixed in, cooked on a flat pan until slightly charred. Thicker and heavier than Indian roti; the coconut adds texture and slight sweetness. Eaten for breakfast or as a snack with sambal.

snacks.name: Kavum (Oil Cake)
ingredients: Treacle (or kithul palm treacle -- the Sri Lankan version)
instructions: Kavum are the Sri Lankan oil cakes eaten at New Year (April)
Made from rice flour with kithul treacle (the Sri Lankan palm sugar)
Fried in hot oil -- they puff slightly
The kithul treacle gives a deep caramel flavor
Made specifically for the Sinhala and Tamil New Year -- the auspicious sweet
The oil cakes symbolize prosperity
snacks.description: Sri Lankan New Year oil cakes -- rice flour with kithul palm treacle (deeply caramel) and coconut milk, fried in hot oil. Made for the Sinhala and Tamil New Year (April). The oil cake symbolizes prosperity. Kithul treacle is a uniquely Sri Lankan palm sugar.

desserts.name: Watalappam
instructions: Melt jaggery with a little water over low heat, strain to remove impurities, and cool.
Beat eggs well and mix with coconut milk.
Add the cooled jaggery syrup, cardamom, nutmeg, and rose water. Mix until smooth.
Pour the mixture into a greased steaming dish. Sprinkle cashews on top.
Cover tightly with foil and steam for 40-45 minutes until set.
Allow to cool completely before serving.
Serve chilled, cut into wedges.
desserts.description: A rich Malay-influenced coconut custard pudding made with jaggery, spiced with cardamom and nutmeg. A festive dessert especially popular during Ramadan.

desserts.name: Watalappan (Coconut Custard)
ingredients: Jaggery or kithul treacle (the Sri Lankan palm sugar)
instructions: Watalappan is the Sri Lankan steamed coconut custard
A Malay-influenced dessert brought by the Malay community to Sri Lanka
The Malay community: brought as soldiers and servants to Sri Lanka under Dutch and British colonization
Kithul treacle: the dark palm sugar that gives watalappan its deep caramel flavor
The custard is steamed (not baked) -- the gentle heat of steam prevents curdling
The texture: silky, firm, slightly jiggly -- like a very good flan
Topped with cashew nuts
desserts.description: Sri Lankan Malay-heritage steamed coconut custard -- coconut milk, kithul palm treacle (dark caramel palm sugar), eggs, cardamom, and cloves steamed (not baked) until silky and firm. Brought by the Malay community (Dutch and British colonial soldiers). Kithul treacle is uniquely Sri Lankan.

desserts.name: Kiri Pani (Coconut Cream with Treacle)
ingredients: Thick coconut cream (kiri: the top layer of pressed coconut)
instructions: Kiri pani is the simplest Sri Lankan dessert -- but deeply satisfying
Kiri: the first press of coconut milk -- thick, almost solid
Poured into a bowl
Kithul treacle poured over -- the dark amber palm syrup
The coconut cream swirls with the dark treacle
Eaten by dipping with bread or just eaten with a spoon
desserts.description: Sri Lankan coconut cream with palm treacle -- thick first-press coconut cream in a bowl with dark kithul palm treacle poured over. The simplest and most satisfying Sri Lankan sweet: two ingredients, remarkable together. Eaten by spoon or with bread.

drinks.name: King Coconut Water (Thambili)
instructions: Select a fresh king coconut, identifiable by its bright orange exterior.
Using a sharp cleaver, cut the top off the coconut at an angle.
Insert a straw or pour the water into a glass.
Add ice cubes if desired and a pinch of salt to enhance the natural sweetness.
Scoop out the soft, jelly-like flesh from inside to eat as well.
Drink fresh for maximum hydration and nutrition.
drinks.description: Sri Lanka's iconic roadside refreshment. King coconut water is naturally sweeter than regular coconut water and is packed with electrolytes.

drinks.name: Arrack Sour
instructions: Add arrack, lime juice, simple syrup, and egg white to a cocktail shaker.
Dry shake without ice for 15 seconds to emulsify the egg white.
Add ice and shake vigorously for another 15 seconds.
Double strain into a chilled coupe glass.
Dash angostura bitters on top of the foam in a decorative pattern.
Garnish with a lime wheel.
drinks.description: A tropical twist on the classic sour cocktail using Ceylon arrack, a spirit distilled from the sap of coconut flowers. Smooth, citrusy, and uniquely Sri Lankan.

drinks.name: Ceylon Tea
ingredients: Ceylon tea (Uva, Dimbula, or Nuwara Eliya estate)
instructions: Ceylon tea is one of the world great teas -- Sri Lanka is the third-largest producer
Tea estates cover the Hill Country: Nuwara Eliya, Kandy, Dimbula, Uva
The British introduced tea cultivation to Ceylon in the 1860s
The original crop was coffee -- the 1869 coffee rust fungus destroyed all the coffee
James Taylor planted the first commercial tea in Loolecondera Estate (1867)
Uva: the east side of the mountains -- slightly astringent, malty
Nuwara Eliya: the highest elevation -- delicate, floral
Dimbula: the west side -- bright, brisk
Ceylon high-grown tea is the most prized
drinks.description: Sri Lankan estate tea -- Ceylon tea from the Hill Country estates (Uva: astringent, malty; Nuwara Eliya: high-grown, delicate; Dimbula: bright, brisk). Britain introduced tea in the 1860s to replace coffee (destroyed by 1869 fungus). James Taylor planted the first estate. Third-largest world tea producer.
